recommendation: Pass the initial elements to the HashSet constructor as an array instead of using collection initializer syntax.
Replace the LINQ call with a loop or with a method of the collection type, especially in frequently-updated code.
Check the Count, Length or IsEmpty property instead of calling Any(). If the variable is declared as IEnumerable, use a type that knows its length, such as an array or List.
Use Array.Empty instead of allocating a new empty array, or [] if your C# compiler supports collection expressions.
Index the collection directly instead of calling ElementAt. If the collection doesn't support indexing, use one that does, such as an array or List.
Use the Count or Length property instead of calling Count(). If the variable is declared as IEnumerable, use a type that knows its length, such as an array or List.
Use Array.Exists or List.Exists instead of Any(predicate). If you look up elements often, store them in a HashSet or Dictionary.
Use List.Contains or Array.IndexOf instead of the LINQ Contains. If you search the collection often, store the elements in a HashSet.
Use Array.TrueForAll or List.TrueForAll instead of All(predicate).
Index the last element directly, for example array[^1] or list[list.Count - 1], instead of calling Last().
Index the first element directly, for example array[0], instead of calling First().
Check that the collection isn't empty and index the first element directly instead of calling FirstOrDefault.
Check that the collection isn't empty and index the last element directly instead of calling LastOrDefault.
Check the index against the Count or Length property and index the element directly instead of calling ElementAtOrDefault.
For arrays whose element type implements IEquatable, compare them with AsSpan().SequenceEqual() instead.
Replace BinaryFormatter with a supported serializer such as JsonUtility, System.Text.Json, or DataContractSerializer, or write the data manually with BinaryReader and BinaryWriter.

Add the readonly modifier to the member, or to the get accessor if the property also has a setter. Without it, the compiler copies the whole struct before every call through an in parameter, a readonly field or a ref readonly reference. Omit the modifier only if the member is meant to modify the struct.

Add the readonly modifier to the called member if it does not modify the struct. Otherwise pass or hold the value by ref instead of in or readonly, or copy it into a local variable once before the calls, so the compiler does not make a hidden copy on every call.

Add [AutoStaticsCleanup] to each static field, automatic property and event that must be reset on code reload or when entering Play Mode, and declare the type and all its containing types partial. Add [NoAutoStaticsCleanup] to static members that must keep their value.

Follow the guidance in the issue description. Usually this means removing readonly from the static member so that it can be reset, or adding [NoAutoStaticsCleanup] to it if its value stays valid across code reload.
Declare the type and all its containing types partial so that the cleanup code can be generated.

Add [AutoStaticsCleanup] to this static member if it must be reset on code reload or when entering Play Mode, and declare the type and all its containing types partial. Add [NoAutoStaticsCleanup] if it must keep its value.
Remove the static constructor. Initialize static members with field initializers or in an [OnCodeLoaded] method instead.
If this is a static constructor, move the assignment to an [OnCodeLoaded] method. If this is an instance constructor, make sure the constructed object can't outlive the current code load scope.
